blocks.x: Okay, let's get everybody's name. What is your right name?
My right name is Irving Lionel Reason.
Yes, I never knew the Irving. I just saw that in the phone. That's a place name. And where Alway, by the way?
Well, we're in Baton Rouge.
Yeah, and what's the address here?
This is 3012 Newton Street.
And today is, let's see, it's late in May. What is today's date?
27th day of May.
27th day of May, 1981.
And can I have your name?
My name is Joel Gardner.
Is it picking you up okay?
Yeah.

Good, and my name is Dick Allen. We've got a directional mic there, so we have to check and see if it'll pick up everybody else. I understand. Yeah. Well, anyway, I wanted to ask you a lot of questions about Paul Barnes, nicknamed Polo, because you've already been interviewed before by a lot of other things. And I went through his journal.

When did you first meet Paul? I met Paul in 1929 in New Iberia, Louisiana. I was playing with a band under the leadership of Beauregard Adams, an alto player. And the name of the band was the Nighthawks, a six-piece band. And during that time, times were pretty tough. So we were working on these $2, $2.50, $3.00 night jobs. And I had been with them about a year. And I knew the whole territory by going around with this little band. And, in fact, I came to New Iberia on a freight train. It was during the Depression, and everybody traveled around on a freight train. And Paul D. Barnes had a band with Nellie Lutcher and Kermit Scott and Elris Joseph, a drummer, and quite a few others. I can't recall their names right now. Their bass player, Chester, lived in New Orleans, now has no Chester's last name. And they had a big band. In fact, they had one of the best bands in the whole territory. But they couldn't find work because they were playing special arrangements. And that Creole session down there hadn't begun to understand what special arrangements were. And Paul D. Barnes was writing the arrangements. And he and I became friends. And he asked me to come go with them on a few jobs. And I went with them and showed them different places at Sheraton Beach, around Generate, different places around where they could meet with different dance hall owners. And I went with them. At that time, there weren't too much dealings with night clubs. It was mostly dance halls. And I went with them. And when they got ready to leave, it was around the carnival season, the Lenten season. And most of the fellas in Paul D. Barnes band went back to Lake Charles, the home of Nelly Lecher, pianist. And I went along with Paul D. Barnes to Homer, Louisiana. And a man by the name of Vincent Lepresto had a jitney dance place. This hall was in Homer, Louisiana. And he talked with Paul D. Barnes. We had played there a couple of times. Paul was about the most popular band leader out in this territory at that time. And Paul went to New Orleans and we got D.D. Pierce. His name is Joseph Pierce. We called him D.D. The trumpet player, Euless Jean, which is trumpet. And we had a drummer that used to be with Sidney Desfene. We called him Shine. Nolan Williams is his right name. Paul was playing alto sax. And he got another saxophone player from Idaho, who is also deceased now. My name is Sammy Johnson. And we started to play on Wednesdays and Saturday nights in Homer. And we'd play on Sunday nights for the American Legion. And Monday nights we'd play spot dance jobs around Morgan City, Thibodeau. And even we went back as far as New Iberia and played dance. We had a smaller band then, but we played more stock arrangements and head arrangements instead of the organized special arrangements. And we stayed there. In fact, Paul stayed there about a year. And he went back with King Oliver's band. That was early thirties. And he joined King Oliver's band. Let me see, they were in Huntington, West Virginia. And after being there, about a couple of months, he told King Oliver about me. And I had met Louis Armstrong in New Orleans, but he didn't know too much about me. And Paul joined King Oliver's band. And they were working in Portsmouth, Ohio. That's where King Oliver's bus burned up. And over half of the musicians quit King. And Charlie Turan was the pianist. And he quit and married a woman who had seven children in Portsmouth. And he quit the music game. And just started working around Portsmouth. Very good musician. And they sent for me. And I kept the telegram about four weeks. I didn't know how to leave Louisiana. I had never gone out of Louisiana in my life. And so we had, after I received the telegram, they sent it to New Orleans, then they forwarded it to home Louisiana. And I met with Professor Ernie, who has a music store. He's now retired in Lafayette, Louisiana. He had a band, and he was also teaching bands in different public schools. And I showed it to him, and he and I were very good friends. And he said to me, he said, man, you can always come back to Louisiana and make three dollars a night. He said, this is a good experience for you. And I said, well, I think I'll do that. I was teaching music in Homer, Louisiana at that time and playing with the rest of the band after Paul left. Because we were making more money even at that time, the three and four dollars a night, than the musicians around New Orleans were making. And I left. And I went with King Oliver, and I stayed with him about three years. Then Paul left first, and came back home. And a little later on, the band was just about going down. And I left the band, came back to New Orleans. And I got a job working at the same night. I just went by the same bass player. I was trying to call his name a while ago, Chester's Chester's Artist. I think that's the name.
Oh yeah, I know him. Well, they had a band.

And the nighthawks on Roman and Kodai. And the club owner's name was Peter Tato, a tagging fella. And he had a color fella, was the manager named Peter Robinson from Mississippi. And I sat in with the band. During that time, Fetch Wilder's style was very popular. And I used to sing and play like him. And that first night I sat in with the band. And the manager called me on the side and asked me, I would like to work there. So I told him, Noah, he said, I'd like to make you the leader of the band. I said, well, I wouldn't want that. I said, I'll tell you, when you get rid of this band, then you call me and I'll choose my own man. See, they were playing more like on a big band style, which was different from Fetch Wilder's style. And I knew I had to train them. And I got, I hired Paul D. Barnes to play clarinet. I didn't want them to play sax, because Fetch Wilder's style then was clarinet and trumpet and chord rhythm, bass, piano, guitar and drums. And I worked there, oh, I guess about eight, seven, eight months. Then King Oliver sent for me to come back to the band, see if I could revamp the band. I went back to King Oliver's band. And I joined him in Savannah, Georgia. And we got on the road. And he had, it was just about the last round up then. He had a bunch of musicians. The band was a raggedy band. And not only musically, but clothes-wise too. I guess I had the only decency in the whole band. And I looked through the arrangements, and they were all messed up. And so I told King, I said, the only thing I can do, because I was an arranger then, I said, I'll have you just write you a whole new repertoire. So we continued to try and, try to revamp the band and doing a little bit of rehearsing. And we bought some orchestrations. And I saw where things had gotten so, so bad. And these fellas just didn't have it as being professional musicians. The name of King Oliver up. And we played a dance in Vicksburg, Mississippi. And when we played this dance, I met a woman. And I told her, I said, I'm going to leave this band. She said, well, when you going? Where you going? I said, I'm going back to New Orleans. I said, after this dance is over tonight, I'm coming by your house. I said, don't you tell anybody. And I'm not going to let King Oliver out talk me. And we played out in a place they call the park. And when I got finished, she had a little old call there. And I put my clothes in there and went on to her house. And I stayed there about two or three days. And after King Oliver, he had, he was a pretty wise fella. He knew just about what had happened. And I got free trained. Came and went back to New Orleans. Yes. And this day that I got into New Orleans, I went where Joe Robichaux was playing. Have you heard of Joe Robichaux?
Oh, I never heard.

Yeah. Well, he was always a rescue for me from the first time I came to New Orleans. He was like a guiding angel. And so he told me, he said, My, my boys in my band want you to play with the band. He said, and all I'll do, I'll do, I'll just, um, um, wipe the doors and attend to the business. He said, because I don't like to play much anymore. Because Joe used to like to gamble anyhow. And he before doing that, when I began to get older, then play. And he said, you can play all these special arrangements. And, uh, Porter was in the band. Uh, Eugene Porter and Eugene Ware, Bucket. Uh, no, Freddie Coleman was playing drums with him. And Bucket was with the other, another, a pretty small band drummer. And, uh, Gishard, Alfred Gishard was with him.
His brother was with him.

Dennis Gishaw was playing bass, Samuel Dutre was playing tenor, we had another alto player, we used to call him Singary for nickname, he went to Cincinnati, I forget his name. Singary? Singary. We called him Singary for the cigarette. I don't know him. He was great alto player, well he and Gene Porter were close, and so they went on the boat. I left, I went with, I didn't go in the band, he said Don Albert is here. I said Don Albert has a bigger band and they're doing much traveling and he needs you much more than I do. He said, but if you don't make it with Don, he said, you got a job here with me. And now Tootie, the Italian fellas, two brothers of them, they owned the Rhythm Club, that's where Joe was playing on the regular six night a week job back there on Jackson Avenue, right off Cleveland. And so Joe Rubishow got Don Albert on the phone and Don said, well I want you to meet me at ten o'clock. That was placed on Rapport Street. The original name was Astoria, but they had changed the name upstairs to Tick Tock. And when we got off, when Joe finished playing that night, instead of me going right home, I got with Samuel Dutry and those Italian brothers who owned the Rhythm Club. And they used to have this wine in great big barrels in those days, just around and then screw it and pour it and enjoy it out. And we sat there talking until about five o'clock that morning and drinking that Italian wine. And we walked from there, I was living on drives and Felicity, some folks call it Felicity. I was living right in front of Kaufman's store. Sam and I went to my house and we laid across the bed at twelve o'clock and the next day we were still sleeping. Jim Johnson, the bass player with Don Albert, he and Alvin Alcorn knocked on my door. And we were still laying up there sleeping. And he said, man, Don was waiting. He said, we tried about six different piano players. Pichon, Bonnie El-Saint-Diego, Jeanette Kimball. He said, we tried them all. He said, but they don't fit down there, I was banned. I said, well, we'll be down in a few minutes. We just overslept. And we walked down there. When I got to the Tick Tock, they had a fellow from St. Louis was the vocalist. And, uh, his name, Buddy Collins. He died while we were on the road. He took sick. He was from St. Louis. And, uh, they had an arrangement on who is Sylvia. Remember that tune?
Mm-hmm.

And, uh, he couldn't get any of them to play. And those were some of his special tunes. He figured they couldn't play that. They couldn't play anything else he had. So, when I went there, uh, I was still half asleep. So, he said, uh, play this for me. And, uh, I said, which, I said, this is the arrangement? He said, yeah. I said, man, I'm ready to rehearse right now. Let's go. And I went on it. And Don jumped up and Don, he said, this is what I've been trying to get you fellas to do all day. And the band is going to race. And I went on with Don. And I stayed with Don until 1939. And in 1939, we were working, uh, in Detroit on location. Uh, um, with, uh, at the, uh, Club Plantation, 555 East Adams Street. And, uh, I didn't like the salary. We had played in, in, in Indianapolis, Indiana. And, uh, uh, Joe Mitchell, Italian fellow owned the club there. And he told me, he said, look, anytime you want to leave that band, see, write me a postcard or send me, or call me, do anything, you see. And I sent for you to come. And I left, um, Don Alva's band. I gave him a two weeks notice. And I quit and went to Indianapolis, Indiana. And I sent back to New Orleans. And I took part of Joe Robey, she was being in there. And I sent for Sam Dutre, but Sam didn't want to come. He had, he was tied up with, um, uh, money and the bus. He had some money, it was willed to him, from, uh, Nora Dutre, his trombone player, from Chicago. And it will sound a lot of money. And he loaned Joe Robey showed some money to buy a new bus. And he didn't want to leave his money behind. And, uh, so he sent Seaman Jefferson, clarinet player. Uh, Dennis Gishard, those two. And Gene Ware, our trumpet player. Those three came up to, um, I sent for them. And they came to Indianapolis, Indiana. We worked on that one job until the first of, uh, 42. And, um, a fella got killed from the place. And they closed the place down. They didn't, he didn't, didn't take us off Saturday, but it was no more business. And I, I went to work with a band out of Grand Rapids. And, uh, Grand Rapids, Michigan. And while working with this little band, uh, Freddie Coleman and Ruben Hughes and Saul Broad, a Jewish fella. They came, they called New Orleans looking for me. And, uh, they said, he's in, last time we heard about Lionel, he was in Indianapolis, Indiana. So they contacted Indianapolis, Indiana, Union. And, uh, this union referred them to the Grand Rapids Union. And they said, yes, he's waking out here at the Celebrity Club. And, uh, they didn't even call me. They came up, Freddie Coleman, uh, Saul Broad and Ruben Hughes. They said, man, we need you bad in Detroit. They said, we had a band over here, over there. And the local boys, the half or half of the band, and they're fixing to go on a regular location. They had all of the arrangements. So they quit after rehearsing. The Detroit boys quit. And they were gonna pick up three more boys. And they were going on the job. He said, now, if you can come with us. I said, well, how many pieces are you gonna use there? He said, uh, we're gonna use six pieces. I need a bass player. I need a tenor saxophone player. And bass player and a tenor saxophone player. And I need you. I said, well, I'll tell you, when you go to Indianapolis, Indiana, and you get, you ask for, uh, I think this boy's name was Joe Williams. And, uh, ask for Seaman Jefferson. He was my tenor sax. And, uh, I'll meet you tomorrow evening in Detroit. When they got to Detroit, I had written three arrangements. I was ready for rehearsal. I sat up that night, and I wrote enough arrangements for that six piece band to keep us rehearsing two weeks. And that saved the day for us there. I stayed there. Freddie Coleman came back to New Orleans. And I was, um, um, I went, I went to the Army. I was inducted into the Army from this same job in 1943. I went in, went, they sent me to, uh, Battle Creek, Michigan. I stayed in Battle Creek, Michigan. They kept me there about six weeks playing with the, um, the MP band. And, um, I left, they sent me down to Aberdeen Proving Ground, Maryland. And when I got down there, um, I stayed there from 43 until April the 12th, 1946. They sent me to school for the mechanic. And after three and a half weeks, they, um, changed that. My MOS and sent me to, um, another school for the clay typists. And after my four weeks was up, they sent me on the field for field training down in, um, just below Richmond, Virginia. And, um, when I came back, the, uh, first sergeant said, I was, uh, the reason, pack up your, um, fatigues, check it in, check out your, uh, khaki suit, check out and, and, uh, just, um, get another set of khakis and another set of ODs and go to detachment E. For the duration of the war and one year after. That's just about two city blocks from where I was trained at.
Uh huh.

I was set there as an entertainment director. All of this other stuff. Uh huh. This is up in the air. And that's one of the big acts that, um, President Roosevelt did for that ordinance camp. Nobody was supposed to be assigned there. It's a school. Hardin' a school. Even my, uh, CO wasn't assigned, but he never did get shipped. And I was assigned there because this was, uh, the, the, uh, the beginning of the integration then. Uh huh. Trying to integrate the armed forces. And I was one of the GOATs and I didn't know it. Uh. I stayed there until 46 then biked to, um, to Detroit after I was out of the Army. And from there I came back to New Orleans. And after being there a while, Freddie Coleman and I were working as a duo at the, um, Flamingo. Just down the street. Just down the street. About three, four doors from the famous door. Just right down the street. And, um, during that time, er, I went, I was on a fishing trip and I got lost out then, around October. During the time, er, these tornadoes that hit Louisiana and I was out there for about five days. And, uh, from then on, it was just music, music, until I went to Grunwald. I think that's when you knew me. Yes.
I met you there. We were in music school together. Yeah.

And, um, I was interested in going there because I wanted to take up, um, a, a stuffy stuff They haven't had another lesson since then and they raised their own family and just from what I taught them they became a professional musician. So I see them now, they wanted to call me, they didn't know whether they should call me Mr. Reason. I see that, so one boy by the name of Joe Dutry said, I tell you we're going to call him Pops. And I started those boys off and one of the boys, the little white boy, the young fellow must have been about 15, 15, 16 years old. I taught him clarinet. And when the next year, he was an exceptional student and he went to school here.

at LSU and he made first chair. And he told me that the instructor didn't believe he took music lessons in Liberia. So his daddy said I told him it wasn't New Iberia, it was the man who was teaching it. His name was Aban. Your school and the quality of your teaching. Yeah. And the home, I rented a six room house on Madison Slew. And the man who owned the house sold the house without telling me he was going to sell it. And so I moved to a small single house and I stopped teaching. And I just kept a few students. Then I became the disc jockey for a program over KVIM in New Iberia, Louisiana. And some of my students that I taught to encourage them on Saturday mornings at 10 o'clock, I would have them on live. They were youngsters, 18, 18, 12. I'd have them to play and sing. It was just an impromptu show. And when this was, while I was doing that, I went back to work to play at a place called the Victory Club. Well, the club owner came and asked me why was I throwing my time away when I could be making $300 or $400 a week. So I went over there and started working with him. And then I kept my little evening show because that was just one hour, four to five until I decided I wanted to go to California. So I went down to California. And I went to Los Angeles. The same week I got there, I joined the Local 47. And they earned, it was $150 to join the union. So I gave them $150 and my transfer card. And they told me I had to wait 90 days before I could go to work regular. And I could do casuals. And I used to go down to the union every day. And you could get a reservation through one of the rehearsal rooms. And I went out practicing. One day I was practicing. I never forget I was playing our arrangement on. I ain't got nobody. And a wingy man on. You ever hear of you? Oh yeah. I met him. Well, he looked, he opened the door. Look at that night. He said, hey cousin. I said, I heard that music out there. I ain't waiting around here like that. He said, where are you working? I said, I'm not working anymore. I'm supposed to wait 90 days. Only thing I can pay is a casual. So he said, come on with me. And at that time the president of the union was President Tigroy. And he took me upstairs. And he made me acquainted with the president. And he called him. He said, look, he said, this is my cousin from New Orleans. He said, I want him in my band. And so Tigroy asked him, he said, what's the gentleman's name? He said, he's no gentleman. He's a musician. He said, he said, well, how long has this musician been in town? And then he said, well, he been in a few weeks. So the president told him, he said, I didn't hear that. I don't want to hear it. He said, tell my secretary to come in here and bring his card with him. He took my card. He tore it up. And he gave me another card. And that meant I had been in Los Angeles over two years. And I had been doing other work. And I had been doing other work. This was off the record. Doing other work, working with my cousin in a restaurant. So I went to work with Wingy. Then Wingy saw about my town. Put me in the band. Jack T. Gordon was in the band. I can't remember the other fellas. And he made me the leader of his band. And he took me down to Johnny Mercy's office. And he told Johnny Mercy's office. He said, I brought this New Orleans man here with me. He said, he's piano playing my band. He writes a lot of songs. He said, I want you to do something for him. So Johnny said, well, right now, he said, I'm tired up. And my health is not too good. He said, I'm fixing to go over to Hawaii. He said, I'm going to be over there for a few weeks. And when I come back, he said, I'll give you a call. And when I was on my way out, his lieutenant, I can't remember his name. And he said, leave your telephone number and address here with the secretary. And about two hours after I got home, the telephone rang. There was Johnny Mercy on the phone. He said, I didn't want to do business with you through Winky Men Home. He said, you're a writer. You don't need to go through anybody. So he gave me an appointment to come back. And I went back to his office and talked to him. So he gave me a job checking compositions. And he said, I'm going to go through the office. But people would write. They'd bring them. They always wanted Johnny Mercy to check the song. And he wasn't interested in that anymore. He had the Palm Springs Publishing House then. And so he said, everything that doesn't look good, throw it in 513. Try his best. And so he advised me. He said, now we have a lot of folks come here with songs. They're not written right. They're, they are, some of them are too long to be commercial. He said, the secretary will give them your home number and let them go to your house. Then you can rewrite the song for them. Then you'll be part of the song. So I did, I started doing that. And I still worked in the band with Johnny. With Winky Men Home. And so, Winky carried me all over. He got pictures, everything done for me. And he told me about Kiddowry. Having a contract for the Benny Goodman story. And he said, Kiddowry needs you. You don't need him, but he needs you. Because some of the fellas had quit. And, did you ever meet Don Mule? E-W-E-L-L. Do you know him? Sure. Well, he had quit. Ory. And I went to work with Ory. When I got there, they brought me the same story that King Oliver gave me. We lost our music in the fire. We need you to write that stuff over. So, Ory hummed whole arrangements to me. That's the kind of memory Kiddowry had. Hummed the trumpet part. The clarinet part. And I set my piano at my little, I had a little, one room apartment up on 226 and a half, East 69th Street. And, uh, I bought a, uh, used piano for $25 and had it tuned up. And I used that for my practice and to, for these compositions. And Ory sat at the piano. And, uh, uh, uh, he hung these parts to me. And I make the arrangements for them. Then we recorded for Good Times Yes.
Do you have that album? Uh, some of them are at the university, yeah. I think there's three of them.

Yeah. All right. Now, and we did another one for Verve at the All Star. And it was supposed to be one that would go into, uh, what they call a capsule. Mm-hmm. So, I don't know if it had been released or not, but I noticed, I got a letter about a few weeks ago from the union. And, um, they told me to, uh, search into it. All right. Uh, about, um, that, that recording session. Because there may be money for me. Mm-hmm. Because, uh, I was working in, when they were doing it for the Verve, I was working in Medford, Oregon. And they sent it there for me. And I came down. And I had to do all the arrangements, one number at a time. As I write it, we record it. Mm-hmm. And from Monday until Friday of that week. Mm-hmm. We recorded that session about fifteen numbers. Who was on the session? That's referred. Um, I got those pictures around. I was looking for them this morning. Mm-hmm. All right. Um, um, um, Ory. He's a Spanish-American boy. What's his name now?
What does he play? Clarinet. Phil Gomez. Mm-hmm.
Clarinet. Um, did you remember this? Clarinet. The trumpet player played the horn in the movie with Jack Webb, the color fellow.
Was he with Ory before Teddy Buckner? That's the man I'm talking about.

Teddy Buckner. Teddy Buckner is the man. Yeah. Well, Teddy Buckner, uh, they had Teddy Buckner on trumpet. Mm-hmm. And, um... Well, we can, I can look it up. Yeah. And I can't remember, but it's on the Verve label. Mm-hmm. And, um, I'll never forget, and we had a lady. They imported from Paris, France to sing Kid Ory's, uh, song, His Flavor. And she did it in both, um, French and English. Little that would have been. Yeah. And, um, I had to first sit down and write for her to get her keys right. And, um, the way this arrangement was done, anybody couldn't write for Ory. Mm-hmm. You had to really know his musical ability. See, Ory wasn't a fast reader, like Louie. Mm-hmm. It wasn't a fast reader. So you had to know how to write, and write it simplified, that they could take it and do what they want with it. Mm-hmm. And, and, and they had tried about three or four different bands with Ory, and they didn't, they couldn't do it. And so, uh, somebody recommended me, and Ory said, yes, I forgot about Lionel. They said, I thought he was back in Duonga, but right there in Medford, Oregon. Mm-hmm. And, uh, and I wrote that stuff for them. So they paid me double for everything. Mm-hmm. Everything they paid me double for. And Ron took it on the, um, on the plan. And when I got back to Medford, where I was playing at the, at Hotel Medford, uh, that Friday night when I got there on the plan, um, is Danny. Danny Martin, Martin. He was an Italian from Brooklyn, New York. Mm-hmm. They were all shaking my hand and everything. Then I was getting ready to go back up to my room. He said, um, Ford, don't forget your, your shirt, and your boxing. That's it.
I didn't wake this week, you see, the hotel guy to have a celebrity. He said we'd pay you even though you weren't here. So I stayed there until almost a year.
Can I ask you a couple questions about Paul Monson? I keep forgetting things, you know.
And if we're finished with Ori there.
Well, did you and Nelly Lutcher ever play two pianos together? Yeah.

It was two pianos. See, what they had, a lot of places where, it wasn't a long, long time in Gay from Ingrace. But at Sharon's at the Beach there were two pianos. So Nelly was playing one side to another. During that time was the same time when Underneath the Harlem Moon came out. You remember that song? Oh, sure. That's the year.
That's the year. Milt Brewer Rhythm had a hit on that, I think, with Ori and the Rhym. Can I tell you? I guess it was. Yeah.
And that was one of his features.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah.
And so y'all would play at the two pianos. Not four hands on one piano, but two separate pianos. Two separate pianos.
Yeah.

And who were the Southern Syncopators? Do you remember that band? Well, the Southern Syncopators, they were from New Orleans. I think that was Sidney Desvigny. I see. I get all these things mixed up. Yeah, Sidney Desvigny.
Now, this drummer that I told you a while back that we got to play with us in Homer, his name was, we used to call him Shine.
Yeah.
But Shine's right name was Nolan Williams.
Mm-hmm.
And he was the drummer with the Southern Syncopators.
I see. Yeah. And then, then who was Alan Prade? Alan Prade was the vocalist in Paul D. Barnes' band.

I see. He was a great big guy. He was fat, huh? Oh, yeah. And he didn't have electric loud speakers in those days. He used a little megaphone. Like Joe Lawrence used to do with Papa Celestine. Mm-hmm. He was about two blocks away. And he was from St. Martinville. Mm-hmm. Right out of New Iberia. Eight miles out of New Iberia.
No, I see.
And during that time, Bum Johnson was living in New Iberia. Mm-hmm. And another drummer by the name of Chayee, who used to be a drummer with Papa Celestine.
Oh, I hear him, too.
He died, I think.
A little bit of a fella. Yeah. Yeah. And he was with Punch for a while. That's right.
That's right.
Anyway, did you mention Shelley Lamelle? I know we talked about him. That's Shelley Lamelle was with us.
Yeah. And the band was with Paul Head with Niddy Luschen.
Mm-hmm.
That was one of the trumpet players. Used to live downtown below Lone Avenue. Yeah.
Now, let's get this straight. Euless John was there, Shelley Lamelle and Diddy. That's right.
Yeah.
Were they all there at once, or did they have two, or how did that work? No.

segments.title: Interview opening: names, place and date
segments.summary: Allen gets Reason's full name, the Baton Rouge address and date, introduces Joel Gardner, and checks the microphone.

segments.chapter: Early years with Paul Barnes and King Oliver
segments.title: Meeting Paul Barnes in 1929, the Homer band, and joining King Oliver
segments.summary: Reason tells how he met Barnes in New Iberia while with the Nighthawks, played with Barnes's band in Homer, Louisiana, then followed Barnes to King Oliver's band after the bus burned.

segments.chapter: Early years with Paul Barnes and King Oliver
segments.title: Nighthawks club in New Orleans, rejoining and leaving King Oliver
segments.summary: Back in New Orleans Reason leads a Fats Waller-style small band, then returns to a ragged Oliver band in Savannah and slips away after a Vicksburg dance.

segments.chapter: Don Albert, Detroit and the Army
segments.title: Joe Robichaux's band and the Rhythm Club
segments.summary: Joe Robichaux welcomes Reason back and lists his sidemen; Reason is pointed toward Don Albert and spends a night drinking wine with Robichaux's players.

segments.chapter: Don Albert, Detroit and the Army
segments.title: Joining Don Albert, Indianapolis, and the Detroit sextet
segments.summary: Reason wins the job with Don Albert on an arrangement, stays to 1939, then leads a band in Indianapolis, works in Grand Rapids, and writes arrangements for a Detroit six-piece before induction.

segments.chapter: Don Albert, Detroit and the Army
segments.title: Army service at Aberdeen and return to New Orleans
segments.summary: Reason describes his Army years at Aberdeen Proving Ground as entertainment director, then postwar work in Detroit and New Orleans.

segments.title: Teaching in New Iberia, then Los Angeles with Wingy Manone, Mercer and Ory
segments.summary: Reason teaches music and does a radio show, goes to California, gets into Local 47 through Manone, works for Johnny Mercer, and writes arrangements for Kid Ory.

segments.title: Writing and recording Ory's arrangements while based in Medford
segments.summary: Reason recalls the Verve session with Ory in which he wrote each arrangement as it was recorded, and the Medford hotel job.

segments.title: Playing two pianos with Nellie Lutcher
segments.summary: Allen asks about Reason and Nellie Lutcher playing two pianos at Sharon's at the Beach.

segments.title: Southern Syncopators and drummer Nolan Williams
segments.summary: Allen asks about the Southern Syncopators; Reason says Shine, Nolan Williams, was their drummer.

segments.title: Alan Prade the vocalist and New Iberia drummers
segments.summary: Reason describes Barnes's big singer who used a megaphone and drummers around New Iberia, including one from Celestin's band.

segments.title: Trumpet players in Barnes's band: Shelley Lamelle, Diddy and Euless Jean
segments.summary: Allen and Reason sort out which trumpeters played when, including who was in Homer.

segments.title: Creole language and Reason's family background
segments.summary: Asked about French and Creole, Reason says his mother's family was Creole and gives her maiden name.

segments.title: Alan Prade as front man of Barnes's band
segments.summary: Reason says the vocalist was the band's entertainer in front and Barnes was its brain.

segments.title: Nellie Lutcher's family band and drummer Elric Joseph
segments.summary: Reason names Lutcher's brothers and father in Lake Charles and tells of Elric Joseph, whom he later sent for in Indianapolis.

segments.title: Barnes's advice on seasoned musicians and four-beat drumming
segments.summary: Reason relays Barnes's advice to hire seasoned players and criticizes younger drummers who play two beats to the bar.

segments.title: Drummer Alonzo Stewart
segments.summary: Reason and Allen talk about Alonzo Stewart's drumming, his neck surgery and a recent session.

segments.title: Reuben Hughes and the Baruch family's Club Zombie
segments.summary: Reason explains Saul Broad as the owner of the nightclub where they played.

segments.title: Saxophonist Al Wilson and Cormick Scott
segments.summary: Reason confirms Al Wilson played with Nellie Lutcher and names another player from Texas.

segments.title: Nighthawks personnel under Beauregard Adams
segments.summary: Reason lists the members of the Nighthawks and their roles.

segments.title: Barnes and his saxophonists doubling on clarinet
segments.summary: Allen and Reason discuss Samuel Johnson as Barnes's understudy and Barnes playing clarinet and later soprano.

segments.title: A church pianist and the Bulls Club
segments.summary: Reason tries to recall a piano player who played in churches and taught school.

segments.title: Alton Purnell, Reason's cousin
segments.summary: Allen mentions Purnell and Reason says he is his cousin, who came to the West Coast in 1954.

segments.title: Alex Lutschaw, Barnes's cousin and student
segments.summary: Reason says Barnes taught his cousin, who left music for a religious group.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: Second reel: getting a union card through Manuel Mineta
segments.summary: After the reel change, Reason tells how Barnes took him to the union secretary, who loaned him the dollar for a card.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: The alto player who lost the Aspen house job to Walter Pichon
segments.summary: Reason and Allen try to name an alto player who was on early Armstrong recordings and lost a job to Pichon.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: King Oliver's business troubles and booking agent Ross McConnell
segments.summary: Reason says Oliver neglected business, his agent skimmed money, and Oliver's widow's royalties are discussed.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: Blue Mondays in 1948 and King Oliver's decline
segments.summary: Reason recalls hosting Oliver's wife and the later health decline of Oliver, who told him he was the last New Orleans musician he would send for.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: How King Oliver played
segments.summary: Reason describes Oliver's endurance, mouthpiece practice, rhythm choruses and breathing technique.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: No recordings but regular radio broadcasts
segments.summary: Reason says the band never recorded and discusses the unpaid radio broadcasts in the towns they played.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: Army camps and theaters
segments.summary: Allen asks if the band played Army camps or theaters; Reason says camps came after 1941.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: The Dodds brothers and Chicago clubs
segments.summary: Reason recalls Johnny and Baby Dodds living across from his family in New Orleans and a Chicago club.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: The Oliver band bus wreck and Ross McConnell's money
segments.summary: Reason tells how Oliver's bus went off a West Virginia mountain, Oliver's back was hurt, and the band was stranded.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: Band uniforms with Oliver
segments.summary: Reason says they wore uniforms at first and then regular suits.

segments.chapter: Union, New Orleans and King Oliver
segments.title: Drummers Raymond Williams and Raymond Howell
segments.summary: Allen asks about two drummers; Reason says Howell was with Oliver, hired in Hopkinsville.
